practice_items.prompt: Which validation strategy defines exactly what valid input looks like and rejects everything else, rather than trying to enumerate every bad pattern?
options: Denylist (blocklist)
Allowlist (whitelist)
Output encoding
Canonicalization
practice_items.explain: Allowlisting defines the known-good shape of input and rejects anything that doesn't match; it does not need to anticipate every attack variant.

practice_items.prompt: Select ALL statements that correctly describe why client-side (JavaScript) validation is not a security control.
options: A browser is entirely under the attacker's control, so JavaScript checks can be disabled or bypassed
An attacker can send a crafted request directly to the server with a tool like curl, skipping the browser entirely
Client-side validation must still be re-enforced on the server for any security-relevant check
Client-side validation is cryptographically enforced and cannot be bypassed
practice_items.explain: Client-side validation only improves UX; because the client is attacker-controlled, every security-relevant check must be re-verified server-side.

practice_items.prompt: An application validates a raw, un-decoded path string before checking it for '../' sequences. Why is this a mistake?
options: It has no effect on security
It makes the application faster
An attacker can URL-encode the traversal sequence (e.g. ..%2F) so it slips past the raw-string check, then gets decoded later, this is a canonicalization bypass
Only client-side code is affected
practice_items.explain: Validating before canonicalizing (decoding/normalizing) lets encoded or obfuscated payloads bypass the filter; the correct order is decode/normalize first, then validate.

practice_items.prompt: Name the security concept that transforms data at the point it is inserted into a new context (HTML, SQL, shell) so special characters are treated as literal data, not code.
practice_items.explain: Output encoding/escaping is applied at each output context, since the correct transformation differs between HTML, SQL, shell, and JSON.

practice_items.prompt: SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), and command injection share what root cause?
options: They all require physical access to the server
The application trusted that input was 'just data' when a downstream interpreter treated part of it as code or control syntax
They only affect encrypted connections
They are unrelated vulnerability classes with no common cause
practice_items.explain: In all three, unvalidated input reaches an interpreter (SQL engine, browser, shell) that treats some of its characters as executable syntax rather than literal data.

practice_items.prompt: Which practice eliminates SQL injection risk regardless of what input validation is or isn't done upstream?
options: Parameterized queries
Verbose error messages
Running the app as root
Hardcoding secrets in source
practice_items.explain: Parameterized queries bind user input as data, never as SQL syntax, closing off injection independent of validation.

practice_items.prompt: Select ALL reasons secrets (API keys, passwords) should NOT be hardcoded in source code.
options: They remain visible in version control history forever, even if later removed
Rotating a compromised secret requires a code change and redeployment
They are automatically encrypted by the version control system
Anyone with repository read access can see them
practice_items.explain: Hardcoded secrets persist in history, require a code change to rotate, and are visible to anyone with repo access; version control does not encrypt file contents.

practice_items.prompt: An authentication check throws an unexpected exception. Secure coding says the application should:
options: Grant access anyway so the user isn't blocked
Ignore the exception silently and continue
Log the user in as admin
Deny access by default (fail securely/fail closed)
practice_items.explain: Failing securely means an unexpected error must never accidentally grant access; deny by default.

practice_items.prompt: Name the principle that says application processes and database connections should run with only the minimum access they need to function.
practice_items.explain: Least privilege applies to running code and service accounts, not just human user accounts.

practice_items.prompt: Why is pinning and patching third-party dependency versions considered a secure-coding practice, not just a maintenance task?
options: A vulnerability in any dependency becomes a vulnerability in the whole application, so unpatched dependencies are unpatched attack surface
It has no security relevance
It only affects build speed
Dependencies cannot contain vulnerabilities
practice_items.explain: Modern apps are built on many third-party libraries; an unpatched vulnerable dependency is a real vulnerability in the shipped application.

practice_items.prompt: Which testing approach reads an application's source code without executing it?
options: DAST
Fuzzing only
Penetration testing
SAST
practice_items.explain: SAST (static application security testing) parses source code directly and never runs the program.

practice_items.prompt: Select ALL statements that correctly describe the tradeoffs between SAST and DAST.
options: SAST can run before the code is even merged, giving very early feedback
DAST requires a running, reachable instance of the application
SAST tends to produce more false positives because it cannot always confirm attacker-controlled input reaches a flagged line
DAST can see every code path in the application, including rarely-used admin features
practice_items.explain: SAST runs early and over-flags because it lacks runtime context; DAST needs a live instance and only sees the paths it actually exercises, not every code path.

practice_items.prompt: A dynamic scanner sends a crafted request to a live login form and observes that it can bypass authentication. What kind of finding is this?
options: SAST-only, since it's about code logic
DAST, since it required interacting with the running application
Neither, since automated tools cannot find this
A compiler warning
practice_items.explain: DAST tests the running application from the outside, exactly the way this scenario describes.

practice_items.prompt: Name the kind of security testing that is performed by a skilled human who chains findings together and reasons about business logic flaws automated SAST/DAST tools cannot recognize.
practice_items.explain: Penetration testing is human-driven and can reason about business logic in ways automated scanners cannot.

practice_items.prompt: Why do mature CI/CD pipelines typically run BOTH SAST and DAST rather than picking just one?
options: SAST and DAST are the same tool with different names
Running both is required by law in every jurisdiction
DAST always finds a superset of what SAST finds
They find largely non-overlapping vulnerability classes, so together they give broader coverage
practice_items.explain: SAST sees the code but not runtime behavior; DAST sees runtime behavior but not the code, they complement rather than duplicate each other.
